source_message.text:
A few additional thoughts after months of refining this direction that may help:

The biggest realization is that the signature of the brand is no longer just the accent over the É—it's the entire **V language**.

The larger opening V should be the hero of the wordmark. The smaller closing V and the É accent should all be derived from that same geometry. Together, these three elements should share identical angles, proportions, and material language. Ideally, if someone covered every other letter except the two Vs and the accent, it should still feel unmistakably like VELLVÉ.

The remaining letters should support the V rather than compete with it. The strongest direction we found was treating them as architectural objects instead of typography—quiet, sculptural, and intentional.

Some additional refinements I'd love to explore are:

• Perfecting the kerning so the word reads as one unified mark rather than "VE LL VÉ."
• Making the Ls feel more structural than typographic. We gravitated toward taller, architectural proportions with subtle custom geometry rather than decorative serifs.
• Refining the É accent so it feels like a brand signature rather than punctuation—slightly shorter, thicker, and more integrated with the V geometry.
• Exploring subtle internal reveal lines or dimensional details that create depth without feeling ornamental. The logo should feel like it could exist as a beautifully crafted brass or stone sign, where light naturally catches the details.

One important realization was that the logo became too severe when we leaned too heavily into architecture. I still want it to feel timeless and sculptural, but with a sense of warmth, vitality, and aspiration. We found that warmth came from the material expression—champagne metal, light, subtle illumination, and depth—not from softer or more decorative typography.

Please feel free to challenge the typography, but preserve the design language. I'm more interested in refining the DNA of the wordmark than introducing entirely new ideas.

Ultimately, I don't think this project is about creating a beautiful font. It's about creating a proprietary wordmark that feels inevitable—as though VELLVÉ could never have been written any other way.

If there's one thing I'd love to achieve, it's this: the opening V should eventually become recognizable enough to stand on its own as a long-term brand asset, without ever needing a separate icon or monogram. The wordmark itself should become the identity.

value_updates.material_role: Introduce warmth, vitality, light, subtle illumination, and depth while preserving a timeless, sculptural character
value_updates.style_constraint: Material expression should provide warmth rather than softer or decorative typography

source_message.text:
Thank you for taking a step back and exploring the V first. I think that's exactly the right direction. I'd like to continue exploring the V before moving back to the full wordmark, because I believe that's where the identity of the brand will be established.

For now, I'd like to continue working entirely in black and white. The champagne metallic treatment is still part of the long-term vision, but I don't want color influencing our decisions yet. Let's solve the geometry first. The material should enhance the design, not define it.

The right arm of the V deserves much more exploration. Rather than feeling like another stroke of the letter, it should become an integral part of the V's construction. I'm interested in exploring changes in proportion, width, length, and termination that make it feel intentional without becoming decorative.

The beauty should come from proportion, geometry, and construction—not added details. Every design decision should feel structural rather than stylistic.

I also don't want us to lose sight of the bigger objective. If someone erased the letters ELLVÉ, the first V should still feel unmistakably like vellvé. That's the level of distinction I'm hoping we achieve. Once we solve that, I believe the rest of the wordmark will follow naturally.

Hi Abdulbari,

I think this is the strongest version yet. The optical drawing approach made a significant difference, and the letterforms now feel much more cohesive as a family.

I'd like to begin exploring the material and color treatment while we continue refining the wordmark.

I'm attaching this image only as inspiration for the champagne gold color and finish—not the 50/50 black and gold split. I'm drawn to the richness, warmth, and subtle metallic quality of the gold, and I'd love to see how that material language could be incorporated into the VELLVÉ wordmark.

I don't have a predetermined solution in mind, so I'd love to see your interpretation. My only goal is to preserve the timeless, architectural feel we've been building while introducing a refined champagne gold that feels luxurious rather than flashy.

Hi Brittany,

Here is a material exploration grid showing our locked optical wordmark rendered across four champagne gold finishes inspired by your reference!
